new_statements.quote: Betonung. 11. Im Ful herrscht der Starkton. Er liegt stets auf der vorletzten Silbe des Wortes. Die Silbe mit dem Starkton, sowie auch die vorangehenden Silben desselben Wortes haben außerdem Hochton, dagegen die letzte Silbe, also die auf den Starkton folgende, wird tieftonig gesprochen. Die Regel ist also einfach diese: Alle Silben mit Ausnahme der letzten haben Hochton, die vorletzte hat neben dem Hochton noch den Starkton, die letzte Silbe ist tieftonig. Die meisten Wörter, die von dieser Regel abweichen, weisen sich schon dadurch als Fremdwörter aus.
new_statements.translation: Stress. 11. In Ful the dynamic (strong) accent prevails. It always lies on the penultimate syllable of the word. The syllable with the strong accent, and also the preceding syllables of the same word, additionally have high pitch, whereas the last syllable, i.e. the one following the strong accent, is spoken with low pitch. The rule is thus simply this: all syllables except the last have high pitch, the penultimate has the strong accent in addition to the high pitch, the last syllable is low-pitched. Most words that deviate from this rule thereby reveal themselves to be loanwords.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dynamic stress (Starkton) always falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; all syllables before and including the stressed one are high-pitched, the final syllable low. Enclitic monosyllables count as part of the word, so stress moves right to remain penultimate in the word-plus-clitic unit. Words that break the rule are mostly loanwords.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; Westermann explicitly says there is no separate sentence stress beyond each word's Starkton (p. 198).
new_statements.exceptions: 'Die meisten Wörter, die von dieser Regel abweichen, weisen sich schon dadurch als Fremdwörter aus' (loanwords); enclitic monosyllables shift the Starkton rightwards so that it stays penultimate in the word+clitic unit, and the newly stressed syllable often lengthens while a preceding long vowel may shorten (o díli togore vs o dilí nde); deviations are marked with an accent in the book (p. 198).
new_statements.domain_note: Word ('Silbe des Wortes'); the rule is restated for the phonological word including enclitics: 'einige einsilbige Wörter.. werden enklitisch behandelt.. deshalb rückt der Starkton vor und ruht nun auf mi, so liegt er also wieder auf der zweitletzten Silbe dieser Worteinheit' (p. 198). Westermann also says he observed no separate sentence stress: each word's Starkton is equally prominent (p. 198). Contradicted by later Nigerian-Fulfulde descriptions reported second-hand in Breedveld 1995:130-132: Arnott 1965:78 (Gombe) = initial with exceptions; McIntosh 1984:20 (Kaceccereere) = last non-final CVC/CVV syllable, else initial; Breedveld's own reanalysis = last heavy syllable with final extrametricality in nouns, else initial.
new_statements.identity_note: Westermann 1909 describes the Fula 'in und um Sokoto' (informant Audu Hamadu of Sokoto, recorded in Lomé 1907; Vorwort p. iii). Sokoto Fulfulde belongs to ISO fuv / Glottolog nige1253 (Hausa States Fulfulde; alt. name Kano-Katsina-Bororo Fulfulde), although Glottolog does not list Westermann 1909 among nige1253's references and the earlier west2454 (Western Niger Fulfulde) check filed the same pages there; Miyamoto 1989:17-18 (Sokoto dialect study) treats Westermann 1909 as the principal reliable source on Sokoto Fula. Klingenheben 1927 (Die Laute des Ful, Google Books snippets in the west2454 folder) criticised Westermann's Hausa-speaking informant, so the 1909 data may carry Hausa interference. The second-hand modern statements concern other fuv dialects: Arnott 1965/1970 = Gombe; McIntosh 1984 = Kaceccereere (Nigeria). Taylor 1921 (also held by the project) is Adamawa Fulfulde = adam1253/fub, already in the catalog via Stennes 1967.

readall_conflicts: Neither listed work could be opened, so no new first-hand statement was obtained; the conflicts below are among material already held by the project in our check folder. (1) Westermann 1909 §11 pp. 197-198 (Sokoto informant; held by the project verbatim) says the Starkton 'liegt stets auf der vorletzten Silbe des Wortes', every syllable but the last is high, the last is low, deviations are loanwords, and enclitics re-compute the penult ('o nāmi' vs 'o nāmi di') with the stressed vowel often lengthened — this reads as fixed: penultimate syllable with a fixed H..HL tone contour, not weight-sensitive, so the existing_statements label 'weight-sensitive' for Westermann is not what his text says. (2) Arnott 1965:78 (Gombe dialect, quoted second-hand in Breedveld 1995:130) puts stress on the first syllable of nearly all polysyllables, with exceptions (numerals, adverbs, interrogatives, negative verb forms). (3) McIntosh 1984:20 (Kaceccereere, southern Zaria, quoted second-hand in Breedveld 1995:132): 'In nominals, [stress] generally occurs on the last non-final CVC or CVV syllable. In the absence of such a syllable, the initial syllable of the nominal is stressed, regardless of its structure', and she declines to give a rule for verbs (1984:82). Breedveld (Maasina, but with a Yola consultant) argues that Arnott's initial-stress rule comes from equating high pitch with stress, and that the true rule is stress on the last heavy syllable (final syllable extrametrical in nominals), els…

sources.note: 'Im Ful herrscht der Starkton. Er liegt stets auf der vorletzten Silbe des Wortes' (p. 197); all syllables except the last are high, penult also carries the Starkton, last syllable low; deviating words are mostly loanwords; enclitic monosyllables (di, nde, mi etc.) join the preceding word and the Starkton moves right to stay penultimate in the unit (o naami vs o naami di), often with vowel lengthening on the newly stressed syllable; no separate sentence stress observed (p. 198). Copied from the west2454 check folder (HathiTrust uc1.$b380782 public-domain text view downloaded via r.jina.ai).

sources.note: ADAMAWA dialect (adam1253/fub), not fuv — kept as a neighbouring-variety control: 'The accent is predominantly a stress accent, and, generally speaking, depends on the long vowels'; disyllables: long/diphthongal first vowel takes it, otherwise 'the accent is even'; negative past and nogas 'twenty' final; trisyllables: long penult stressed, else first; polysyllables usually penult unless a long vowel attracts it. Also notes a Sokoto negative form windai with final accent.
